atoms.name: Distance vector idea
atoms.one_line: Each router keeps a vector of costs to all destinations and sends it only to neighbours. Update is Bellman-Ford.

atoms.name: Updating a vector from neighbours
atoms.one_line: New cost to t is the minimum over neighbours v of c(x,v) plus v's advertised cost to t; the arg-min is the next hop.

atoms.name: Rounds and convergence
atoms.one_line: Info moves one hop per round. Good news (cost drop) spreads fast; bad news (failure) spreads slowly.

atoms.name: Count-to-infinity and fixes
atoms.one_line: After a failure two routers feed each other stale routes and costs climb. Split horizon, poison reverse, and a small infinity (RIP 16) limit it.

atoms.name: Link-state flooding
atoms.one_line: Each router floods its neighbour costs to everyone; all routers end with the same map. Flooding one LSA costs 2E-(V-1) transmissions.

atoms.name: Dijkstra at a router
atoms.one_line: Grow a tree from the source by settling the nearest unsettled node; the first hop of each tree path is the forwarding entry.

atoms.name: DV versus LS and protocols
atoms.one_line: LS: whole map, Dijkstra, faster convergence, more computation, transient loops. DV: neighbours only, loops can persist. RIP is DV (hop count), OSPF is LS.

patterns.name: DV table update and next hop
patterns.note: Add link cost to neighbour vector, take the minimum, note the next hop. Stale vectors after failures are the trap.

patterns.name: Count-to-infinity and loop probability
patterns.note: Loop forms if the stale update arrives before the failure update: race of exponential timers.

patterns.name: Unused links under shortest paths
patterns.note: All-pairs shortest paths; mark links that appear on no path; then change weights and repeat.

patterns.name: DV versus link state: algorithms and properties
patterns.note: Bellman-Ford versus Dijkstra; RIP versus OSPF; split horizon limits; convergence. UDP/TCP/BGP details are outside the named 2027 list.

traps: Using the neighbour with the smallest advertised cost and forgetting the link cost to that neighbour.
Applying a failure instantly at every node; news travels one hop per round.
Believing split horizon removes all loops; it only fixes two-router loops.
Forgetting to include the cost to reach the neighbour (c(x,v)) in the Bellman-Ford sum.
Marking only heavy links as unused; always compute all-pairs shortest paths.
Counting flooding transmissions as E instead of 2E-(V-1) (duplicates are still transmitted).
Swapping DV and LS with Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra.
Reading INCORRECT statement questions as which are true.
Treating OSPF as inter-domain or TCP-based; it is an intra-domain protocol carried directly over IP.
blueprint.summary_md:
**Payoff:** simulate routing updates and tell distance vector from link state in seconds.

- **Update**: neighbour's vector plus link cost, take the minimum.
- **Failure**: bad news crawls and can count to infinity.
- **Dijkstra**: link state builds the full map, then settles nearest first.

$$D_x(t)=\min_v\,[\,c(x,v)+D_v(t)\,]$$

Next: try the Level 1 questions.
blueprint.summary_full_md:
## Distance vector
Each router stores a vector with its best known cost to every destination. It sends the vector to its neighbours only. When $x$ receives $v$'s vector, it recomputes
$$D_x(t)=\min_v\,[c(x,v)+D_v(t)],$$
and the minimising neighbour $v$ is the next hop for $t$. This is the Bellman-Ford equation applied one step at a time. In synchronous rounds, information about a destination travels one hop per round, so a chain of $n$ routers needs $n-1$ rounds.

## Good news and bad news
When a link gets cheaper, the better path spreads in a few rounds. When a link fails, routers can keep using stale advertisements. Two routers that point at each other add the link cost to the other's number every exchange, so the cost counts upward: **count-to-infinity**. Fixes:
- **Split horizon**: do not advertise a route back to the neighbour you learned it from. It stops two-router loops.
- **Poison reverse**: advertise it back with infinity.
- A small value of infinity (RIP uses 16) caps the counting.
Loops with three or more routers still need other fixes (hold-down timers, triggered updates).

## Link state
Each router measures the cost to its neighbours and floods a link-state advertisement (LSA) to all routers. Every router builds the same map and runs **Dijkstra**: repeatedly settle the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance and relax its edges. The first hop on each path from the source goes into the forwarding table.

Flooding one LSA over a network with $V$ routers and $E$ links costs $2E-(V-1)$ transmissions: the origin sends on all its links and every other router forwards on all links except the arrival link. Link state converges faster and has no persistent loops, but costs more computation and memory.

## Protocols
**RIP**: distance vector, hop count, infinity 16. **OSPF**: link state, Dijkstra, areas for hierarchy, intra-domain, carried directly over IP. Inter-domain routing (BGP) is not part of this topic.

## Strategy for GATE
1-mark: classify (DV vs LS, Bellman-Ford vs Dijkstra, RIP vs OSPF). 2-mark: one or two rounds of vector updates with a link change, or an all-pairs shortest path check. Write each router's vector as a row and compute one round at a time.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - New cost is min over neighbours of link plus their **advertised** cost.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- To P: 3+7, 2+6, 5+5; **minimum** 8 via Y.
- **To** Q: 3+4, 2+6, 5+8; minimum 7 via X.
- **Answer: B,C**
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't add the wrong neighbour's cost, do add each **link** separately.
hints: Compute R's cost to P via X, Y and Z.
Repeat for Q and note the next hop.
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Topology figure not needed: the three link costs and vectors are in the text.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. To P: via X $=3+7=10$; via Y $=2+6=8$; via Z $=5+5=10$. Minimum 8 via Y. So A (10) is false and C (next hop Y) is true.
2. To Q: via X $=3+4=7$; via Y $=2+6=8$; via Z $=5+8=13$. Minimum 7 via X. So B (7) is true and D (next hop Z) is false.
3. True statements: B and C.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: One iteration only uses the neighbours' current vectors. Results may improve in later iterations, but this question stops after one.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Choosing the neighbour with the smallest advertised distance (Z for P) ignores the cost of reaching that neighbour. Always add the link cost first.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - Loop forms only if P's stale update reaches Q **first**.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- **Q-R** fails; Q learns R is unreachable.
- P still says R is 2 away: a **race**.
- **Answer: 0.5**
pyq_enrichment.explanation: - **Equal** update rates make the race a fair coin.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't assume a loop always forms, do compare send **times**.
hints: Who tells Q about R after the failure?
If P's update arrives before Q's next update, what does Q think?
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. Chain P-Q-R, all costs 1. Before the failure P reaches R at cost 2 via Q; Q reaches R at cost 1.
2. Link Q-R fails. Q sets its cost to R as infinity but has not yet told P.
3. If P's update (R at cost 2) reaches Q first, Q takes it: R via P at cost 3. Now P and Q point at each other: a loop, with counting to infinity.
4. If Q's update reaches P first, P learns R is unreachable and no loop forms.
5. Equal rates mean each order is equally likely: $0.5$.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: The probability equals $\lambda_P/(\lambda_P+\lambda_Q)$, the chance that the next update comes from P. With unequal rates it changes (see the ladder).
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Saying 1 (a loop always forms) ignores that Q can advertise first.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - RIP: distance vector, over **UDP**. OSPF: link state, over IP.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- **I** and II are true for RIP.
- IV is true for OSPF; III is **false**.
- **Answer: C**
pyq_enrichment.explanation: - **OSPF** packets ride directly on IP, not TCP.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't put OSPF on TCP, do put RIP on **UDP**.
hints: Which protocol is distance vector?
Which of RIP and OSPF uses TCP?
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Syllabus note: UDP, TCP and the transport details are not named in the 2027 list. Keep the DV versus link-state classification of RIP and OSPF.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. I: RIP uses distance vector routing: true.
2. II: RIP messages are carried in UDP datagrams: true.
3. III: OSPF does not use TCP; it runs directly over IP: false.
4. IV: OSPF is link-state: true.
5. True: I, II, IV: option C.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: RIP and OSPF are the two standard interior (intra-domain) protocols. For this topic the classification is what matters: RIP gives hop-count distance vector, OSPF gives link state with Dijkstra.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Statement III is the trap: OSPF is not TCP-based. Option B includes it.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - **OSPF** is link state with Dijkstra, intra-domain only.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- A is wrong: **Bellman-Ford** is for RIP.
- C is wrong: OSPF is **intra-domain**.
- **Answer: A,C**
pyq_enrichment.explanation: - Pick the **INCORRECT** statements: A and C.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't read it as which are true, do pick the **false** ones.
hints: Which algorithm does link state use?
Is OSPF between organisations or inside one?
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. A: OSPF uses Dijkstra on a link-state database, not Bellman-Ford. A is incorrect.
2. B: OSPF uses Dijkstra for least-cost paths: correct.
3. C: OSPF is an interior (intra-domain) protocol. Inter-domain routing uses BGP. C is incorrect.
4. D: OSPF supports areas, so hierarchical routing is correct.
Incorrect: A and C.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: OSPF areas reduce flooding scope and routing table size. A backbone area connects the others.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: The question asks for INCORRECT statements. Marking B and D (the true ones) is the common slip.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - Distance vector uses Bellman-Ford; link state uses **Dijkstra**.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- **DV** routers relax with neighbours' vectors: Bellman-Ford.
- LS routers run **Dijkstra** on the full map.
- **Answer: A**
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't swap them, do link LS to the full **map**.
hints: Which algorithm needs the whole graph?
Which algorithm works with neighbours' tables?
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. Distance vector computes $D_x(y)=\min_v[c(x,v)+D_v(y)]$, the Bellman-Ford equation. (i)-(a).
2. Link state floods the whole topology, then each router runs Dijkstra. (ii)-(b).
3. Option A.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: Dijkstra needs every edge cost up front (all-pairs knowledge). Bellman-Ford can run distributed, one relaxation per received vector.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Option C reverses the pairs; the clue is that Dijkstra needs the complete graph, which only link state has.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - Statements one and three hold; **split** horizon fails S2.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- Link state computes a full tree: **heavier** (S1 true).
- **LS** converges faster (S3 true).
- **Answer: D**
pyq_enrichment.explanation: - **Split** horizon does not stop all DV loops.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't trust split horizon alone, do remember three-router **loops**.
hints: Does Dijkstra on the whole graph cost more than one relaxation?
Which protocol converges after fewer exchanges?
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. S1: link state runs Dijkstra on the whole topology (about $E\log V$); distance vector does a cheap relaxation. True.
2. S2: DV with split horizon avoids two-router loops only. Loops with three or more routers can still cause count-to-infinity. False.
3. S3: link state floods the change and every router recomputes at once; DV needs several rounds. True.
4. S1 and S3 true, S2 false: D.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: Link state loops are transient (while LSAs flood). DV loops can persist while the cost counts to infinity.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Believing S2 (split horizon cures loops) gives C. Split horizon fixes only the two-node case.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - RIP is distance vector; OSPF is **link** state.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- **RIP** is the textbook distance vector protocol.
- OSPF floods link states and runs **Dijkstra**.
- **Answer: A**
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't swap them, do tie OSPF to link **state**.
hints: Which protocol uses hop count?
Which protocol floods link-state advertisements?
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Syllabus note: RIP and OSPF are the implementations of the two named algorithms.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. RIP exchanges distance vectors (hop counts) with neighbours: distance vector.
2. OSPF floods link-state advertisements and runs Dijkstra: link state.
3. Option A.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: RIP limits paths to 15 hops (16 means infinity), which also bounds count-to-infinity.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Swapped answer B comes from remembering 'open' as a plain-text protocol. The names do not help; know the classification.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - **Run** all-pairs shortest paths and mark links that appear.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- **Unused**: R1-R2 (6) and R4-R6 (8).
- Both are beaten by 2-hop **detours**.
- **Answer: C**
pyq_enrichment.explanation: - A link is **unused** if every shortest path avoids it.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't use only R1's table, do check all **pairs**.
hints: Is R1 to R2 cheaper directly (6) or via R3 (3+2)?
Is R4 to R6 cheaper directly (8) or via R5 (1+4)?
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Weights read from the figure: R1-R2 6, R1-R3 3, R2-R3 2, R2-R4 7, R3-R5 9, R4-R5 1, R4-R6 8, R5-R6 4. Verified by script.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. R1-R2: direct 6, via R3 $=3+2=5$. Never used.
2. R4-R6: direct 8, via R5 $=1+4=5$. Never used.
3. R3-R5 (9): R3 to R5 costs 9 directly; via R2-R4-R5 $=2+7+1=10$. Used.
4. All other links lie on a shortest path for some pair. Two links unused: C.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: After DV tables stabilise, a link carries data only if it is on some shortest path. Checking every pair is the safe method.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Looking only at links with large weights misses R3-R5 (weight 9), which is still the shortest R3-R5 route.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - **Cheaper** unused links now win; re-run all pairs.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- Both **cheap** links, R1-R2 and R4-R6, now cost 2.
- Both now **used**; R5-R6 becomes unused.
- **Answer: B**
pyq_enrichment.explanation: - Changing a weight can free up a **different** link.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't assume all links become used, do **recheck** every pair.
hints: With R4-R6 = 2, what is R5 to R6?
Is R1-R2 = 2 now a shortest path for R1 to R2?
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Verified by script: only R5-R6 is unused after the change.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. New weights: R1-R2 $=2$, R4-R6 $=2$.
2. R1 to R2: direct 2 beats 5. Used.
3. R4 to R6: direct 2 beats 5. Used.
4. R5 to R6: direct 4, but R5-R4-R6 $=1+2=3$. So R5-R6 is no longer on any shortest path: unused.
5. One link unused: B.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: Lowering an unused link's weight attracts traffic from other links. Here the cheap R4-R6 link makes R5-R6 redundant.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Answering 0 assumes making every unused link cheap makes it used, forgetting the side effect on neighbours.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - Only the **neighbours** N2 and N4 matter.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- **Via** N2: 2 plus N2's vector gives (3,2,.,9,5).
- Via N4: cost 2 plus N4's gives (10,9,.,2,6); **minimum**.
- **Answer: A**
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't update N5 with 6, do use the **new** 2 plus 3.
hints: Who are N3's neighbours?
N3 uses the old vectors of N2 and N4.
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Topology read from the figure: N1-N2 1, N2-N5 3, N2-N3 6, N3-N4 2, N4-N5 4. N3's neighbours are N2 and N4.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. N3's neighbours: N2 (link now 2) and N4 (link 2).
2. Via N2 using N2's vector $(1,0,6,7,3)$: $(3,2,8,9,5)$.
3. Via N4 using N4's vector $(8,7,2,0,4)$: $(10,9,4,2,6)$.
4. Entry-wise minimum with distance to itself 0: $(3,2,0,2,5)$. Option A.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: Only N3 and N2 see the cost change in this round, so N3's new route to N1 and N5 through N2 appears now; other nodes learn about it in later rounds.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Option B keeps the old 6 to N5; the new N3-N2 link makes N5 reachable at $2+3=5$.

pyq_enrichment.quick_method: - N4's **stale** value for N1 plus link: 2 plus 8.
pyq_enrichment.solution:
- N2 says N1 is **infinity**; N4 still says 8.
- **Take** 2+8=10 via N4.
- **Answer: C**
pyq_enrichment.trap_note: - Don't answer infinity, do use the other **neighbour**.
hints: What does N4's vector say about N1 in this round?
N3 has two neighbours: N2 and N4.
pyq_enrichment.answer_check_note: Verified by synchronous simulation of the stated rules.
pyq_enrichment.solution_full:
1. After the cost change, N3's cost to N1 is 3 (via N2). N1-N2 then fails and N2 sets cost to N1 as infinity at once.
2. In the next round N3 collects vectors: N2 says infinity for N1. N4 (which has not changed) still says $8$.
3. N3's cost via N4 $=2+8=10$.
4. Via N2 would be infinity, so $\min=10$: C.
pyq_enrichment.explanation_full: The route N3 to N4 to N5 to N2 to N1 is stale: it still passes through the failed link. This is the first step of count-to-infinity; the path really is unreachable.
pyq_enrichment.trap_note_full: Answering infinity applies the failure to N3 instantly. Information about the failure needs a round per hop.

ladder.stem: Which shortest-path algorithm is the basis of the **distance vector** routing algorithm?

options.text: Dijkstra
Bellman-Ford
Floyd-Warshall
Kruskal

hints: Distance vector routers use only neighbours' tables.
Which algorithm relaxes edges using other nodes' distances?
Dijkstra needs the whole graph.
ladder.solution:
- DV uses neighbours' **estimates** to relax.
- That is the **Bellman-Ford** equation.
- **Answer: B**
ladder.quick_method: - **DV** is Bellman-Ford; link state is Dijkstra.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't pick Dijkstra, do remember it needs the full **map**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A distance vector router knows only its neighbours' vectors.
2. It computes $D_x(t)=\min_v[c(x,v)+D_v(t)]$, which is one Bellman-Ford relaxation.
3. Dijkstra needs every link cost, which only link-state routers have. So B.
ladder.explanation_full: Kruskal builds minimum spanning trees, a different problem. Floyd-Warshall is all-pairs and centralised.
ladder.trap_note_full: Dijkstra is the best-known shortest path algorithm, so it feels right; but it needs the whole graph first.

ladder.stem: In link-state routing, a router sends information about its **own links** to

options.text: only its direct neighbours, to be added to their tables
all routers in the network, by flooding
a central server only
only the destination router

hints: Link state aims to give every router the full map.
Who needs each router's link costs?
Flooding reaches everyone.
ladder.solution:
- Every router needs the whole **map**.
- So each **LSA** is flooded to all.
- **Answer: B**
ladder.quick_method: - **LS**: own links to everyone. DV: whole table to neighbours.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't mix with DV, do recall DV sends **much** to few.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Dijkstra at each router needs the cost of every link.
2. Each router therefore floods a small advertisement (its own links) to all routers.
3. So B. Option A describes distance vector, which shares whole tables with neighbours only.
ladder.explanation_full: LS: small message, to everyone. DV: large message (whole vector), to neighbours only. That contrast is a standard exam item.
ladder.trap_note_full: Option A is the distance vector behaviour.

ladder.stem: In distance vector routing, each router sends its distance vector to

options.text: all routers in the network
its directly connected neighbours
only the router with the shortest path
only the next hop

hints: Distance vector never sees the whole network.
Who does a router talk to directly?
Neighbours.
ladder.solution:
- DV talks to **neighbours** only.
- Knowledge spreads **hop** by hop.
- **Answer: B**
ladder.quick_method: - **DV**: whole vector to neighbours only.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't flood, do share with **neighbours**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A DV router has no map of the network.
2. It sends its whole vector of costs to each directly connected neighbour.
3. News about far destinations arrives one hop per exchange. So B.
ladder.explanation_full: This hop-by-hop spread is why DV converges slowly and why it can count to infinity after a failure.
ladder.trap_note_full: Option A describes link state flooding. DV never sends to routers it does not share a link with.

ladder.stem: The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) measures the cost of a path by

options.text: link bandwidth
hop count
round-trip delay
number of routers with high load

hints: RIP is a distance vector protocol.
Its metric is very simple.
What is 16 hops in RIP?
ladder.solution:
- RIP counts **hops**.
- Sixteen hops means **unreachable**.
- **Answer: B**
ladder.quick_method: - **RIP** metric is hop count, infinity is 16.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't pick bandwidth, do pick **hops**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. RIP is a distance vector protocol with the simplest possible metric: the number of hops.
2. A cost of 16 is treated as infinity, so RIP supports paths of at most 15 hops.
3. So B.
ladder.explanation_full: Bandwidth-aware metrics belong to protocols like OSPF (cost per link) and EIGRP. RIP's limit on 15 hops is a deliberate cap on count-to-infinity.
ladder.trap_note_full: OSPF costs can reflect bandwidth, which is why bandwidth feels plausible. RIP does not look at it.

ladder.stem: The **count-to-infinity** problem occurs in

options.text: distance vector routing after a link failure
link state routing after a link failure
both, equally often
neither, since both use shortest paths

hints: Which protocol shares only neighbours' estimates?
A router can believe a stale route from a neighbour.
Costs keep growing round by round.
ladder.solution:
- Stale **estimates** feed each other.
- Costs **climb** by the link cost each time.
- **Answer: A**
ladder.quick_method: - **Count-to-infinity** belongs to DV.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't blame link state, do recall it **floods** the failure.
ladder.explanation: - Link state recomputes from the true **map**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. In DV, a router trusts what neighbours say, even if that route runs back through itself.
2. After a failure, two routers can advertise routes through each other; each increases the other's cost.
3. Link state floods the failure and every router recomputes from the real map, so the problem does not arise. A.
ladder.explanation_full: Link state has only short transient loops while the flooding completes. They disappear once all routers have the same map.
ladder.trap_note_full: Option C: link state can loop briefly but never counts to infinity.

ladder.stem: Router R has neighbours X, Y, Z at link costs 2, 5 and 3. Their advertised costs to destination P are 9, 3 and 6. After one distance vector update, R's cost to P is ______.
hints: Cost via X is $2+9$.
Compute via Y and via Z in the same way.
Take the smallest.
ladder.solution:
- **Via** X 11, via Y 8, via Z 9.
- Take the **minimum**: 8.
- **Answer: 8**
ladder.quick_method: - **Minimum** over $v$ of $c(R,v)+D_v(P)$.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't pick Y's 3 alone, do add the **link** cost 5.
ladder.explanation_full: The neighbour with the smallest advertised distance is Y (3), but Y is also the most distant link. The sum decides.
ladder.trap_note_full: Choosing Z (smallest link cost plus smallest advertisement: 3 and 6) or Y without adding gives 6 or 3, both wrong.

ladder.stem: Router R has neighbours X, Y, Z at link costs 2, 5 and 3. Their advertised costs to destination Q are 4, 7 and 2. Which neighbour is R's next hop for destination Q after one update?

options.text: X
Y
Z
X and Z tie

hints: Cost via X is $2+4$.
Compute via Y and Z.
The next hop is the argmin.
ladder.solution:
- **Via** X 6, via Y 12, via Z 5.
- **Z** wins with 5.
- **Answer: C**
ladder.quick_method: - **Next** hop is the neighbour that gives the minimum.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't pick the nearest link, do pick the cheapest **sum**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Via X: $2+4=6$.
2. Via Y: $5+7=12$.
3. Via Z: $3+2=5$.
4. Minimum 5 via Z: next hop Z.
ladder.explanation_full: Both parts of the routing-table entry (cost and next hop) come from the same minimisation. A forwarding table stores only the next hop.
ladder.trap_note_full: X has the cheapest link (2) but Z's advertised distance to Q is so small that Z wins overall.

ladder.stem: A network has links A-B 4, A-C 2, B-C 1, B-D 5, C-D 8, C-E 10, D-E 2, D-F 6 and E-F 3. The shortest distance from A to F is ______.
hints: Settle nodes in order of distance, starting at A.
A to C is 2, then B through C is 3.
Then D, E, and F.
ladder.solution:
- **Settle**: A 0, C 2, B 3, D 8, E 10.
- F via E is 13: the **cheaper** route.
- **Answer: 13**
ladder.quick_method: - **Dijkstra**: always settle the nearest unsettled node.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't take the direct A-B edge, do try via **C**.
ladder.explanation_full: The path is A-C-B-D-E-F: costs 2, 1, 5, 2, 3. A greedy 'cheapest edge' walk would not find it; Dijkstra's settling order does.
ladder.trap_note_full: Taking the direct A-B edge of cost 4 gives distance 4 to B, but 3 is possible through C.

ladder.stem: What does the **split horizon** rule say?

options.text: A router never advertises a route back to the neighbour it learned it from
A router advertises every route twice
A router stops advertising after a failure
A router advertises infinity for all routes

hints: It prevents a router echoing a neighbour's own information.
Think about who the route came from.
Do not advertise it back.
ladder.solution:
- Don't advertise a route back to its **source**.
- That removes **two**-router loops.
- **Answer: A**
ladder.quick_method: - **Split** horizon: no echo to the source neighbour.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't confuse it with **poison** reverse, do recall that one advertises infinity.
ladder.solution_full:
1. If B learned a route to C from A, then telling A about it adds nothing useful and can start a loop.
2. Split horizon omits that route from B's advertisement to A.
3. So A. Option D describes poison reverse only for that one route, not all routes.
ladder.explanation_full: Poison reverse is the stronger variant: advertise the route back to the source with cost infinity. Both fix two-router loops but not loops of three or more.
ladder.trap_note_full: Poison reverse advertises infinity back; split horizon is silent. Neither removes every loop.

ladder.stem: Five routers A-B-C-D-E are in a chain with unit link costs. All routers start knowing only their neighbours. Routers exchange vectors in synchronous rounds. After how many rounds does A know the cost to E?
hints: After round 1 A knows B and the neighbours of B.
Information moves one hop per round.
How many hops from E to A?
ladder.solution:
- Info moves one **hop** per round.
- **E** is 4 hops from A.
- **Answer: 4**
ladder.quick_method: - **Rounds** needed equal hops to the destination.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't answer 5, do count **hops**, not routers.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Initially A knows B (1 hop).
2. Round 1: A receives B's vector and learns C (2 hops). Round 2: D. Round 3: D is 3 hops; E enters B's vector only after C learns E.
3. A learns E in round 4: the distance in hops, 4.
ladder.explanation_full: For a network of diameter $D$ hops, all routers know everything after $D$ rounds. This is why DV is slow in large networks.
ladder.trap_note_full: Counting routers (5) instead of hops (4) is the off-by-one.

ladder.stem: Which information does a router put in the link-state advertisement it floods?

options.text: Its full routing table
The costs of the links to its own neighbours
The shortest path to every destination
The list of routers it can reach in two hops

hints: LS shares topology, not tables.
Each router describes only what it measures.
Which data is local and cheap to measure?
ladder.solution:
- A router knows only its own **links**.
- It **floods** those costs.
- **Answer: B**
ladder.quick_method: - **LSA**: my neighbours and their link costs.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't send the table, do send link **costs**.
ladder.explanation: - The LSA carries raw **links**, not computed routes.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Each router can measure only its own links.
2. The LSA lists those neighbours and link costs, nothing computed.
3. Every router then assembles all LSAs into the same map. B.
ladder.explanation_full: LSAs carry sequence numbers so routers drop duplicates and keep only the newest copy. Computed routes (A, C) are what distance vector sends.
ladder.trap_note_full: Option A is what DV sends. LS sends inputs; every router computes its own routes.

ladder.stem: Routers A, B, C, D have links A-B 2, B-C 3, C-D 1 and A-D 7. After DV converges, A's vector is (A, B, C, D) = (0, 2, 5, 6). The cost of link A-D now drops to 1. A and D update that entry at once; then all routers exchange old vectors for one round. A's cost to C is then ______.
hints: D's vector before the round says D to C is 1.
A via D: link 1 plus D's cost to C.
Compare with A via B: 2 plus 3.
ladder.solution:
- **A** via B: $2+3=5$.
- A via D: $1+1=2$; **minimum** is 2.
- **Answer: 2**
ladder.quick_method: - **Good** news: new link plus neighbour's old vector.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't keep the old 5, do re-run the **minimum**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A's neighbours are B (cost 2) and D (cost 1 after the change).
2. B's vector gives B to C $=3$, so via B: $2+3=5$.
3. D's vector gives D to C $=1$, so via D: $1+1=2$.
4. Minimum: 2.
ladder.explanation_full: A cost drop spreads fast: A benefits immediately, and B learns about the shorter path to D and C next round (B via A: $2+1=3$ to D). Compare with failures, which spread slowly.
ladder.trap_note_full: Keeping 5 uses only the old best route. The cost change makes the A-D link attractive.

ladder.stem: Eight routers form a ring, each linked to its two neighbours with cost 1. Each router starts knowing only its direct neighbours and routers exchange vectors in synchronous rounds. After how many rounds does every router know the cost to every other router?
hints: Information moves one hop per round.
What is the largest hop distance between two routers in a ring of 8?
Opposite routers are 4 hops apart.
ladder.solution:
- Info moves one **hop** per round.
- The **farthest** pair is 4 hops apart.
- **Answer: 4**
ladder.quick_method: - **Rounds** needed equal network diameter in hops.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't answer 7, do use the **shortest** way round.
ladder.explanation: - The **diameter** of the ring sets the convergence time.
ladder.solution_full:
1. In a ring of 8, the farthest router from X is the opposite one: 4 hops either way.
2. DV spreads one hop per synchronous round, so a router learns a destination $k$ hops away after $k$ rounds.
3. After round 4 all routers know all costs.
ladder.explanation_full: A round in which no vector changes confirms the tables are stable, so detecting convergence takes one more round. The question asks when the knowledge is complete.
ladder.trap_note_full: Counting around the ring the long way (7 hops) ignores that distance is the shorter path.

ladder.stem: In the network of the previous Dijkstra question (A-B 4, A-C 2, B-C 1, B-D 5, C-D 8, C-E 10, D-E 2, D-F 6, E-F 3), link A-C fails. The new shortest distance from A to F is ______.
hints: Without A-C, A has only one neighbour.
Settle B first at 4, then C through B.
Then continue as before.
ladder.solution:
- A has only **B**: B 4, C 5, D 9, E 11.
- **F** is 14 via E.
- **Answer: 14**
ladder.quick_method: - **Re-run** Dijkstra on the reduced graph.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't reuse the old 13, do **rerun** the algorithm.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A-C is removed, so A's only neighbour is B: $B=4$.
2. Settle B: $C=4+1=5$, $D=4+5=9$.
3. Settle C (5): $D=\min(9,13)=9$, $E=15$. Settle D (9): $E=\min(15,11)=11$, $F=15$.
4. Settle E (11): $F=\min(15,14)=14$.
ladder.explanation_full: The path is A-B-D-E-F, costs 4, 5, 2, 3. A failure changed the first hop from C to B for every destination.
ladder.trap_note_full: Reusing the old path A-C-B-D-E-F through the failed link is the mistake: it cannot be used any more.

ladder.stem: Routers A-B-C are in a chain: A-B cost 1, B-C cost 1. Link B-C fails and B sets its cost to C as infinity. Before B tells A, A sends its table (cost to C is 2). Then B and A alternate updates. B's cost to C after A's second update has been processed is
hints: First: A's table arrives at B: cost to C via A is $2+1$.
Then B tells A: A's cost becomes $3+1$.
Then A tells B again.
ladder.solution:
- **A** sends 2, B sets 3; B sends 3, A sets 4.
- A sends 4, so B **sets** 5.
- **Answer: C**
ladder.quick_method: - Costs **climb** by 2 per exchange pair.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't stop at 3, do follow all three **updates**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Update 1: A sends its cost 2. B takes $2+1=3$ via A.
2. Update 2: B sends 3. A takes $3+1=4$ via B.
3. Update 3: A sends 4. B takes $4+1=5$.
That is A's second update (the third message overall): B's cost is 5.
ladder.explanation_full: B's cost rises 3, 5, 7, ... and A's 4, 6, 8, ... Each router believes the other's stale information. This ends only when the cost reaches the protocol's infinity.
ladder.trap_note_full: Answering 3 counts only A's first update; the question asks after A's second.

ladder.stem: Which statements about link-state (LS) and distance-vector (DV) routing are TRUE?

options.text: LS floods link costs to all routers; DV sends vectors to neighbours only.
DV with split horizon can never form a routing loop.
After a topology change, LS usually converges faster than DV.
LS needs less computation per router than DV.

hints: Think about what each protocol sends and to whom.
Split horizon only prevents two-router loops.
LS runs Dijkstra on the whole graph.
ladder.solution:
- **A** and C true: LS floods and converges faster.
- B false: three-router **loops** survive.
- **Answer: A,C**
ladder.quick_method: - **LS**: more computation, faster convergence.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't trust split horizon alone, do remember bigger **loops**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A: LS floods LSAs to everyone; DV sends vectors to neighbours. True.
2. B: split horizon prevents loops of two routers; loops among three or more can still count to infinity. False.
3. C: LS recomputes everywhere after one flood; DV needs several rounds. True.
4. D: LS runs Dijkstra on the full graph, more work than a DV relaxation. False.
ladder.explanation_full: The trade-off: LS uses more CPU, memory and flooding traffic but converges quickly and has no persistent loops. DV is light but slow and loop-prone.
ladder.trap_note_full: B is the tempting statement; it is true only for two-router loops.

ladder.stem: A network has links 1-2 (4), 1-3 (1), 2-3 (2), 2-4 (6), 3-5 (5), 4-5 (1), 4-6 (3) and 5-6 (7). After all routers learn shortest paths, how many links are never used on any shortest path?
hints: Compute the shortest path tree from every node (or reason edge by edge).
1-2: direct 4 versus 1-3-2 = 3.
5-6: direct 7 versus 5-4-6 = 4.
ladder.solution:
- **Link** 1-2 costs 4 but 1-3-2 costs 3.
- Link 5-6 costs 7 but 5-4-6 is a cheaper **detour**.
- **Answer: 2**
ladder.quick_method: - A link is unused if a **detour** is always cheaper.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't check from one source only, do check all **pairs**.
ladder.explanation: - Compare each link with its best **detour**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. 1-2: direct 4, detour 1-3-2 costs 3. Unused.
2. 5-6: direct 7, detour 5-4-6 costs 4. Unused.
3. 2-4 (6): 2 to 4 via 3-5-4 would be $2+5+1=8$, so it is used. 3-5 (5): 3 to 5 via 2-4 is $2+6+1=9$, used.
4. Other links (1-3, 2-3, 4-5, 4-6) are the cheapest routes between their endpoints. Two unused links.
ladder.explanation_full: A link is on a shortest path for some pair exactly when it is the unique cheapest route between its endpoints (or ties for it). The check is edge by edge.
ladder.trap_note_full: Looking at one source only misses links used by other pairs, for example 3-5.

ladder.stem: Routers A-B-C are in a chain with unit link costs. B-C fails. B sets its cost to C as infinity, but A sends its table first (cost to C is 2). A and B then alternate updates, each setting its cost to the other's advertised value plus 1. Infinity is 16 (RIP). Counting A's first message as update 1, at which update number does some router first reach cost 16?
hints: B's costs go 3, 5, 7, ... on odd updates.
A's costs go 4, 6, 8, ... on even updates.
Which reaches 16 first?
ladder.solution:
- **B** sees 3, 5, 7, up to 15 on odd updates.
- A sees 4, 6, up to 14, then 16: **even** updates.
- **Answer: 14**
ladder.quick_method: - **A** hits 16 at update 14; B needs update 15.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't count to 15 only, do compare **both** routers.
ladder.explanation: - Costs climb by two per full **exchange**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. U1: B=3. U2: A=4. U3: B=5. U4: A=6, and so on.
2. B's values on odd updates: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15; next would be 17 (capped at 16, update 15).
3. A's values on even updates: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16: the 7th even update is U14.
4. The first cost to reach 16 is A's at update 14.
ladder.explanation_full: RIP limits the damage by treating 16 as unreachable, but it still takes 14 updates here. Triggered updates and hold-downs shorten this.
ladder.trap_note_full: Answering 15 assumes B reaches 16 on its 8th update (17 capped at 16 on update 15), but A hits 16 at update 14, one earlier.

ladder.stem: A 3-router chain A-B-C has B-C fail. Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: With split horizon, A does not advertise its route to C back to B.
With split horizon, B never learns a wrong route to C, in any topology.
With poison reverse, A advertises cost infinity for C to B.
Triggered updates make B tell A about the failure at once, shrinking the race window.

hints: Split horizon and poison reverse both concern advertising back to the source.
Does split horizon fix loops of three routers?
Triggered updates send changes immediately.
ladder.solution:
- A, C: split horizon and **poison** reverse.
- **D**: triggered updates shrink the race.
- **Answer: A,C,D**
ladder.quick_method: - **Split**: silent. Poison: infinity. Neither fixes bigger loops.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't accept any **topology**, do check larger loops.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A learned C from B, so split horizon stops A advertising it to B. A true.
2. In the chain, split horizon works. But 'any topology' is false: loops through three routers survive. B false.
3. Poison reverse advertises C at infinity back to B. C true.
4. Triggered updates send the failure immediately, so the stale advertisement has less time to win the race. D true.
ladder.explanation_full: In this chain with split horizon A never tells B about C, so B never gets a false route. The same fix fails in a triangle, where the stale route can come around the loop.
ladder.trap_note_full: Statement B turns a correct rule for chains into a general guarantee.

ladder.stem: Routers A, B, C, D form a square with links A-B 1, B-C 2, C-D 1, D-A 5. Vectors have converged. Link A-B fails; A and B set their entry for each other to infinity at once. Then all routers exchange old vectors for one round. C's cost to A after this round is ______.
hints: C's neighbours are B (cost 2) and D (cost 1).
B's vector now says A is infinity.
D's vector (old) says A is at cost 4.
ladder.solution:
- B says A is infinity; D still says 4: **stale**.
- **C** takes $1+4=5$.
- **Answer: 5**
ladder.quick_method: - **Failures** spread one hop per round; old info still counts.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't answer infinity, do use D's **stale** vector.
ladder.explanation: - D's old route to A runs through **C**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Old vectors: D to A is $4$ (via C-B-A). B to A is now infinity.
2. C's options: via B: $2+\infty$; via D: $1+4=5$.
3. C's new cost to A is 5.
4. The route C-D-C-B... is stale: D's route to A actually goes through C. Next rounds fix it, but count-to-infinity is possible.
ladder.explanation_full: After the failure the real best path to A from C is C-D-A with cost $1+5=6$. C briefly believes 5, and D (using C's new 5) would believe 6 next round: the beginning of a slow climb.
ladder.trap_note_full: Answering 6 (the true distance) skips the effect of stale vectors; answering infinity assumes C hears the failure directly.

ladder.stem: Router S runs Dijkstra on this network: S-A 2, S-B 3, S-C 6, A-B 2, A-D 6, B-D 4, B-E 8, C-E 2, C-D 9, D-F 2, E-F 4. For how many destinations (excluding S itself) is B the first hop on the shortest path from S?
hints: Distances: A 2, B 3, C 6.
D via B is 3+4; E via C is 6+2; F via D.
The first hop is the neighbour that starts the path.
ladder.solution:
- **Tree**: A via A, B via B, C via C.
- D, F go through B: **three** in all (B, D, F).
- **Answer: 3**
ladder.quick_method: - **Count** tree nodes whose path starts with B.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't count only B itself, do include its **subtree**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Settle A (2), B (3), then C (6).
2. D: $\min(2+6, 3+4, 6+9)=7$ via B. E: $\min(3+8, 6+2)=8$ via C. F: $\min(7+2, 8+4)=9$ via D, so via B.
3. First hops: A to A; B to B; C to C; D to B; E to C; F to B.
4. Destinations through B: B, D, F: 3.
ladder.explanation_full: The forwarding table of S has one entry per destination with the next hop, and the shortest path tree is the source of all of them. Subtrees hang from S's neighbours.
ladder.trap_note_full: Counting only the direct neighbour B (answer 1) misses that D and F are in B's subtree.

ladder.stem: A network has 7 routers and 10 links. A router floods one link-state advertisement as follows: the origin sends it on all its links; every other router, on receiving the first copy, forwards it on all its links except the one it arrived on; later copies are dropped but still counted as transmissions. The total number of transmissions for one advertisement is ______.
hints: Sum of degrees is $2E$.
The origin sends on all its links.
Each of the other $V-1$ routers sends on all links except one.
ladder.solution:
- **Total** sent: origin degree plus other degrees minus one each.
- The **formula** $2E-(V-1)$ gives 20 minus 6.
- **Answer: 14**
ladder.quick_method: - **Flood** cost is $2E-(V-1)$.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't answer E, do count both **directions**.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Sum of all degrees is $2E=20$.
2. The origin sends on its $d_0$ links.
3. Each of the other 6 routers sends on $d_v-1$ links.
4. Total $=d_0+\sum_{v\ne0}(d_v-1)=2E-(V-1)=20-6=14$.
ladder.explanation_full: Flooding uses each link at least once, often twice (once in each direction when two routers receive copies at nearly the same time). That is the cost of reliability: no tree is needed.
ladder.trap_note_full: Answering 10 counts each link once, which is a spanning-tree style broadcast, not flooding.

ladder.stem: A chain P-Q-R has all link costs 1. Link Q-R fails. P sends routing updates at rate $2\lambda$ and Q at rate $\lambda$, at independent random times. A routing loop forms if P's stale update (R at cost 2) reaches Q before Q's next update reaches P. The probability of a loop, rounded to two decimals, is ______.
hints: Whose update comes first?
With rates $a$ and $b$, the first event is from the first source with probability $a/(a+b)$.
P's rate is twice Q's.
ladder.solution:
- It is a **race** between two timers.
- **P** wins with $2\lambda/3\lambda$.
- **Answer: 0.67**
ladder.quick_method: - **Loop** probability is $\lambda_P/(\lambda_P+\lambda_Q)$.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't answer 0.5, do weigh by update **rates**.
ladder.explanation: - The faster **sender** is likelier to win.
ladder.solution_full:
1. A loop forms only if P's next update arrives at Q before Q's next update arrives at P.
2. Update times are exponential with rates $2\lambda$ (P) and $\lambda$ (Q).
3. The first event comes from P with probability $\dfrac{2\lambda}{2\lambda+\lambda}=\dfrac23$.
4. $P=0.67$.
ladder.explanation_full: With equal rates this is the 2022 GATE answer, 0.5. The memoryless property of exponential timers makes the race a simple ratio.
ladder.trap_note_full: Using 0.5 ignores that P speaks twice as often.

ladder.stem: Routers A-B-C: link A-B costs 2 and link B-C costs 1. B-C fails and B sets its cost to C as infinity, but A sends its table first (cost to C is 3). Updates alternate A, B, A, B, ...; each router sets its cost to the other's advertised value plus 2. Infinity is 16. Counting A's first message as update 1, at which update does some router first reach 16 or more?
hints: After update 1, B's cost to C is $3+2$.
Each exchange adds 2 to the advertised value.
ladder.solution:
- **B** sees 5, 9, 13; A sees 7, 11, 15.
- B's next value 17 **caps** at 16 on update 7.
- **Answer: 7**
ladder.quick_method: - Costs **climb** by 4 per pair of updates.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't use unit steps, do add the link **cost** 2.
ladder.explanation: - Costs climb by the **link** cost each hop.
ladder.solution_full:
1. U1: B takes $3+2=5$. U2: A takes $5+2=7$. U3: B $=9$. U4: A $=11$. U5: B $=13$. U6: A $=15$. U7: B takes $15+2=17\ge16$, so cost 16 (infinity).
2. The first router to reach infinity is B at update 7.
ladder.explanation_full: Larger link costs make counting reach infinity faster (7 updates, against 14 with unit costs). In RIP all links cost 1, which is why 14 is the usual figure.
ladder.trap_note_full: Counting by 1s (as in the unit-cost version) would give 14.

ladder.stem: A network has links D-F 7, B-D 8, B-C 4, C-E 8, E-F 9, A-C 1, D-E 8, B-E 2 and A-B 7. All routers learn shortest paths, then the weights of all unused links are changed to 2 and the routers re-learn. How many links are unused after the change?
hints: First find the unused links: compare each link with its detour.
Set those to 2 and recompute all-pairs shortest paths.
Which link gets replaced?
ladder.solution:
- **Unused** first: C-E (8) and A-B (7).
- Set both to 2; B-C becomes the **detour**.
- **Answer: 1**
ladder.quick_method: - **Redo** all-pairs shortest paths after each change.
ladder.trap_note: - Don't assume none, do **recheck** every pair.
ladder.solution_full:
1. Initially: A-B (7) loses to A-C-B $=1+4=5$; C-E (8) loses to C-B-E $=4+2=6$. Two links unused (script check).
2. Set both to 2: A-B $=2$, C-E $=2$.
3. B-C (4): B to C via A costs $2+1=3$, cheaper than 4, so B-C is now unused.
4. Every other link is on some shortest path (script check). One unused link.
ladder.explanation_full: A reduced weight on a formerly unused link makes it a better route, which can make a formerly used link redundant. This is the 2010 pattern (2 unused, then 1).
ladder.trap_note_full: Answering 0 assumes cheaper weights make all links used.

flashcards.back: $D_x(t)=\min_v[c(x,v)+D_v(t)]$. The minimising $v$ is the next hop.
Distance vector: Bellman-Ford. Link state: Dijkstra.
Whole vector to direct neighbours only.
Own link costs to all routers, by flooding.

flashcards.front: Rounds for DV to reach a node k hops away

flashcards.back: A cost drop spreads fast; a failure spreads slowly and can count to infinity.
Do not advertise a route back to the neighbour it was learned from. Fixes two-router loops only.
Advertise the route back to its source with cost infinity.
RIP: distance vector, hop count, 16 is infinity. OSPF: link state, Dijkstra, areas, intra-domain.
$2E-(V-1)$ transmissions when each router forwards on all links except the arrival link.
Settle the nearest unsettled node, then relax its outgoing edges.

flashcards.front: Trap: stale vectors after a failure
flashcards.back: Neighbours still advertise routes through the failed link. Use their old vectors in the round.

flashcards.front: Trap: split horizon is not enough
flashcards.back: It fixes loops of two routers. Three-router loops can still count to infinity.
